phases.name: Phase 1, Foundations
phases.goal: Operate a computer like an engineer and write small correct Python programs you can explain without AI.

phases.name: Phase 2, Structures and construction
phases.goal: Choose the structures a junior actually uses, and write code other people can live with. Proofs wait.

phases.name: Phase 3, Professional web systems
phases.goal: Ship a real application once, properly: API, database, frontend, auth, tests, CI, deploy.

phases.name: Phase 4, Interview fluency
phases.goal: Survive a junior loop. Narrated algorithms, systems literacy, and professional readiness through apply.

phases.name: Job-ready Gate A
phases.goal: Pass the exam battery. Competitive for junior / associate SWE at product companies. Not a FAANG guarantee. We do not stop.

phases.name: Phase 5, Proof and full algorithms
phases.goal: Discrete math and the algorithms C5-lite skipped. Starts after Gate A.

phases.name: Phase 6, Computer systems
phases.goal: The difference between a bootcamp graduate and someone who can reason about a machine.

phases.name: Phase 7, Production-scale thinking
phases.goal: Talk about systems the way a mid-level engineer is supposed to, and know what you have not yet lived.

phases.name: Phase 8, Capstone
phases.goal: Run a serious project the way a team would. Program-complete, not job-ready.

Say what a process is at a user level

courses.name: Programming Fundamentals in Python
courses.prereqs: C0 in progress. C1 starts after C0.3 mastered.
resources: Weeks: https://cs50.harvard.edu/python/weeks/ (2024 year URLs 404 as of 2026-08-22; 2022 paths redirect here)
Free CS50 certificate is a program milestone. It is not C1 mastery.
work_types: Midterm and final coding exam, closed-resource
courses.mastery_exit: Independently write, test, and explain an 80 to 150 line program that you designed. The CS50P final project counts. Trace someone else's 50-line function on paper. No AI on the exam. The free CS50 certificate is a program milestone. It is not C1 mastery.
courses.official: Harvard CS50P weeks 0-9 + final project. https://cs50.harvard.edu/python/

courses.name: Command-line tool (project)
courses.prereqs: C0 mastered. C1 in progress (enough Python to write a small tool).
objectives: Specify a CLI tool yourself (not a tutorial clone)
Use Git as the history of the work
resources: Python argparse docs (assigned when we specify)
courses.mastery_exit: A stranger can run your tool from a README. I review it. You fix what I reject.

modules.title: Specify and build a command-line tool

courses.name: Data Structures (pre-gate)
objectives: Implement arrays, dynamic arrays, linked lists, stacks, queues, hash tables, and BSTs
Know when a list beats a hash
Heaps and graphs-as-ADTs move to C2-remainder after the gate
resources: Problem Solving with Algorithms and Data Structures using Python (Miller/Ranum, open)
recommended: Berkeley 61B lectures for ideas (Java .  you watch, you implement in Python)
work_types: Implement each structure from scratch with tests
courses.mastery_exit: Given a problem, you pick a structure, implement the critical operations, state complexity, and name a case where a different structure wins.

courses.name: Software Construction
objectives: FP ideas (immutability, HOFs) without a new language
resources: Official wrap: Missing Semester 2026 Code Quality https://missing.csail.mit.edu/2026/code-quality/
Later official sources named on C8: Missing Semester Packaging and Shipping, Beyond the Code
work_types: Weekly PRs to a course repo I maintain
You review my intentionally mixed PRs
Dual-track assignment (closed, then AI-open and catch the model)
courses.mastery_exit: Submit a PR I would accept on a real team. Closed-resource: write tests for a spec you did not implement.

modules.title: Git II (branch, rebase vs merge, conflict, bisect)

courses.official: MIT Missing Semester 2026 Code Quality + Google Engineering Practices

courses.name: Backend Systems
objectives: Talk to a database without an ORM first, then with one
resources: Official wrap: CS50W https://cs50.harvard.edu/web/ and/or FastAPI official docs
work_types: Schema designs I reject until they are honest
courses.mastery_exit: Design a schema and API for a prompt I have not shown you, implement it, write tests, explain an index choice.

modules.title: HTTP and the web as a system

courses.name: Frontend Systems (TypeScript + React)
objectives: TypeScript as a language, not a linter setting
React as a view layer you understand
Read a TS file you did not write
resources: Official wrap: The Odin Project Full Stack JavaScript https://www.theodinproject.com/
work_types: Rebuild a small UI three times (vanilla → React → against your API)
courses.mastery_exit: Add a feature to a React+TS app I give you that you have never seen. Types stay honest. No AI on the exam.
courses.official: The Odin Project Full Stack JavaScript + Full Stack Open

courses.name: Auth, Quality, Delivery
objectives: Authentication and authorization you could defend
Security checklist for a web app
resources: Official wrap: Full Stack Open remainder + a real deploy https://fullstackopen.com/en/
Later official sources: Missing Semester 2026 Packaging and Shipping Code https://missing.csail.mit.edu/2026/shipping-code/
work_types: Add auth to the C6/C7 app
CI must be green to submit
A break-production drill I run against your URL
courses.mastery_exit: I can create an account, use the product, and you can show me the pipeline, a failing test you wrote, and what you would do if a deploy goes bad.

modules.title: Sessions, cookies, JWT (and when JWT is a mistake)

courses.official: Full Stack Open remainder + a real deploy

courses.name: Intermediate product (project)
courses.prereqs: C6, C7, C8 in progress. Required for Gate A.
objectives: Real Postgres, real API, real auth
README that a stranger can run
Not a todo clone. Not a tutorial
resources: Review notes I write on each submission
work_types: I review it as a hiring manager and as a senior engineer
courses.mastery_exit: I would let a stranger create an account and use it. Pipeline is green. You can defend one tradeoff.

courses.name: Algorithms for interviews (pre-gate)
objectives: A first greedy and a first DP you can narrate
Not NP. Not MST. Not a second algorithms course
resources: A short list of patterns we will actually narrate
courses.mastery_exit: On a new LC-medium-shaped problem, you classify the pattern, implement a correct solution, and narrate complexity without notes.

modules.title: Asymptotics you will say out loud

courses.official: CompSci problem sets. Princeton Algorithms I and MIT 6.006 are post-gate, deferred.

courses.name: Systems literacy
objectives: Dinner-table answers, not a systems course
What DNS, TCP, TLS, and HTTP each do when you type a URL
What "the database is slow" might actually mean
This is a seatbelt. It does not replace C9 to C11
work_types: One oral. If you cannot walk a request from browser to disk, we do not call you job-ready.
courses.mastery_exit: 15-minute closed-resource oral I would not be embarrassed to hear.

modules.title: A process and a syscall in one picture
Where time goes in a web request

courses.name: Professional Readiness A
objectives: A resume that is not a lie
courses.mastery_exit: Resume I would send. You can explain P1 without slides. You have started applying only when I say the work is evidence.

courses.name: Job-ready exam battery
courses.prereqs: P1 accepted. C5-lite, C-syslit, C19a in progress or done. Every job-ready skill at Competent or higher.
objectives: Brownfield change in a foreign repo
Debug a broken app with a hypothesis
resources: The P1 repo for the oral
work_types: Eight exams. All must pass. Completing a course is not a substitute.
courses.mastery_exit: I will say you are competitive for junior / associate SWE roles at product companies and strong startups. It does not mean FAANG L3 is guaranteed. It does not mean we stop.

modules.title: Oral: P1 architecture and a reversed tradeoff

courses.name: Discrete Mathematics
courses.prereqs: C1. Starts after Gate A (or late in search if a loop exposes the hole).
objectives: Write a short proof and spot a fake one
resources: MIT 6.042J Mathematics for Computer Science (OCW) selected chapters + recitations
recommended: Berkeley CS 70 notes for math-in-action examples
courses.mastery_exit: Prove a loop invariant on a program you wrote in C2. Prove a simple graph claim. Refute a wrong induction.

modules.title: Modular arithmetic and a taste of crypto

courses.name: Data Structures remainder
courses.prereqs: C2-lite, Gate A. Heaps and graphs-as-ADTs, plus implement-everything depth.
objectives: Heaps and priority queues from scratch
Graphs as ADTs (rep + traversals you already used in C5-lite, now as structures)
recommended: Berkeley 61B heap and graph lectures (Java .  implement in Python)
courses.mastery_exit: Implement a heap and a graph ADT. State costs. Name when an adjacency list loses to a matrix, and when a heap loses to a sorted array.

courses.name: Algorithms I (remainder)
resources: Official wrap named, not started: Princeton Algorithms I, MIT 6.006
Tim Roughgarden Algorithms Illuminated (selected) or Erickson Algorithms (open)
recommended: Skiena Algorithm Design Manual war stories
courses.mastery_exit: Given a new problem, you classify the paradigm, implement a correct solution, state complexity, and say whether a polynomial exact algorithm is likely.

courses.name: Computer Systems (C)
courses.prereqs: C2, C4. POST-GATE. Starts after Gate A unless a specific loop requires it sooner.
objectives: C memory model; pointers; stack vs heap
Undefined behavior as a real thing
resources: Computer Systems: A Programmer's Perspective (Bryant/O'Hallaron) ch. 1 to 6 selected + labs I adapt
recommended: Nand2Tetris Part I as a 10-hour mental-model module
work_types: A small allocator or binary-format tool
courses.mastery_exit: Draw the stack/heap for a program I give you. Find a memory bug with a method, not luck. Write correct C for a 100-line task.
courses.official: Deferred after Gate A. Not CS50x as C1.

courses.name: Operating Systems and Concurrency
resources: Official wrap named, not started: Operating Systems: Three Easy Pieces (OSTEP)
xv6 book (selected) + a subset of labs (not the whole MIT 6.1810)
work_types: One of: user-level thread package, tiny filesystem, or xv6 lab sequence I designate
courses.mastery_exit: Given a concurrent bug, you form a hypothesis, name the missing invariant, and fix it. You can explain what the kernel did for a read() you wrote.

courses.name: Computer Networking
courses.mastery_exit: Explain a slow API using the network, not the framework. Write a small TCP client/server.

modules.title: HTTP as an application of the above

courses.name: Applied Probability and Linear Algebra
objectives: Probability you will use (Bayes, expectation, tail intuition, hashing/load)
Linear algebra you will use (vectors, matrices, least squares, a taste of embeddings)
resources: Harvard Stat 110 (Blitzstein) selected or Stanford CS 109 notes
3Blue1Brown Essence of Linear Algebra + a short written text
courses.mastery_exit: Compute a real posterior on a debugging/SRE-style story. Multiply and interpret a small transformation. Say what an embedding is without metaphor soup.

modules.title: A little ML math so you cannot be sold nonsense

courses.name: Databases as Systems
objectives: When a document store is honest
courses.mastery_exit: Given a slow query and EXPLAIN, you fix it and say what the planner did. Name an isolation bug in an API you wrote.

courses.name: Security Fundamentals
objectives: Crypto primitives as what they guarantee
resources: A short applied-crypto chapter I assign
work_types: Attack a deliberately vulnerable app (legal, local)
Write a threat model for P1
courses.mastery_exit: Threat-model a feature. Find two real bugs in a PR. Explain TLS's job in one paragraph that is not wrong.

courses.name: Distributed Systems and Data-Intensive Apps
recommended: MIT 6.824 lectures (watch a few; labs optional)
work_types: A small queue/worker system you operate
courses.mastery_exit: Design a system with an explicit consistency and failure story. I will try to break the happy path. You will have already named that path.

courses.name: Software Architecture and System Design
objectives: Light HLD interview fluency after you have opinions from C15
resources: One good design-doc example I provide
recommended: ByteByteGo / Xu after DDIA, for interview shape only
courses.mastery_exit: 45-minute design of a system I name that day. Constraints first. One deep dive. What you measure. What you would cut.

modules.title: Interview HLD as a separate skill

courses.name: Reliability and Observability
resources: Google SRE book ch. 4 to 6, 8, 12 to 15, 17
work_types: Instrument P1 or the C15 worker
courses.mastery_exit: During a game-day, you gather evidence before guessing, name blast radius, and choose rollback vs fix-forward with a reason.

courses.name: Production-style system (project)
courses.prereqs: C15 in progress. C17 may overlap.
work_types: I review it as if it were joining my team
courses.mastery_exit: The happy path is named. I break it. You already wrote that down.

modules.title: Design and operate a production-style system

courses.name: Capstone
courses.prereqs: Job-ready gate + C15 + C16 + C17 (C17 may overlap).
objectives: Run a serious project the way a team would
Not a portfolio demo, a tutorial clone, or a weekend hack
resources: Product requirements; architecture doc; database design; API spec
Testing strategy; CI/CD; cloud deploy; monitoring; security notes; performance notes; user/operator docs
work_types: At least two rounds of code review with me
I score it as a senior engineer reviewing a new teammate's first major deliverable
courses.mastery_exit: I would let this into a real codebase with notes, not a rewrite. Rubric mean ≥ 3.5 and no 1s. A 5 is rare.

courses.name: Professional Readiness B
objectives: Three scored mocks at hire / lean-hire
resources: One real OSS target I approve
courses.mastery_exit: Three scored mocks at hire / lean-hire for junior product-company loops. Resume I would send. You can explain P1 and the capstone without slides.
